items.title: Tesla Hasn't Had a Successful New Product Launch Since JB Straubel Stepped Down
items.summary: 193 points, 246 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (cleantechnica.com)

→ HN comments  ·  193 points  ·  246 comments

Top #1 — Avicebron:

Isn't Tesla trying to be SpaceX's vertically integrated robotics division? My gut feeling says they are trying to move out of the EV business as crazy as that may seem to us normals.

↳ reply 1 — matthewdgreen:

Being in the EV business means having to accept predictable revenues that then tie to more predictable stock prices. Being in the business of "some future technology" doesn't.

↳↳ reply — stymaar:

The big problem for Tesla is that they cannot sustain their valuation from the car manufacturing business. There's a perpetual need to justify why Tesla should be valued an order of magnitude more than other automakers. Selling the dream of future profit is Tesla's main business.

(For the record Tesla makes roughly 10% of Toyota's profits and has almost 3 times the valuation, no Tesla shareholder is ready for a 97% share price drop so Tesla has to keep the dream machine at full steam).

Edit: Tesla is 3 times Toyota in valuation, not 5 as I said earlier, not that it changes the argument much.

↳↳↳ reply — tarsinge:

I don’t know, I think at this point the Tesla stock doesn’t have a link with the company anymore and behaves like any meme coin or collectible token. Like in crypto there is some vague narrative about a crazy future but ultimately the point is only to drive further speculation ("buy it before you’re priced out/join the elite crowd that’ll own the future/etc."). The genius of Elon is having realized (I’d say around the time he tested the ground with pumping dogecoin) that in a stock market where investors don’t buy for dividends but only price speculation the underlying business doesn’t really matter, only the narrative does. Dividends are the only link with the real business, without them the price is only a function of the demand, and what Elon has achieved is maintaining demand through narrative, like in crypto, irrelevant of the company results.

↳ reply 2 — martythemaniak:

Not crazy at all. Tesla gave up being a car company a few years ago, but there's lot of inertia and the 3 and Y are still competitive products in the marketplace.

↳ reply 3 — rurban:

My gut feeling is that they won't selling any cars anywhere anymore because of their CEO. They can either shut it down already, or fire him.

Top #2 — martincsweiss:

There's too many confounders to say that JB Straubel is the cause.

Examples: Covid controversies around musk in 2020, Twitter acquisition in 2022, Musk becoming the world richest person in 2021

Top #3 — xqcgrek2:

Tesla is one china EV tariff away from bankruptcy

↳ reply 1 — jm4:

So is at least half the US auto industry, if not all. Modern Chinese cars look great and you get a lot of bang for your buck. Even without CCP subsidies keeping prices low they would eat up other manufacturers if priced similarly.

↳ reply 2 — modeless:

The Model Y outsells every Chinese EV in China. It's every other US manufacturer who would be doomed if the China EV tariff went away. That's why the 100% tariff was imposed by Biden, not Trump.

items.title: OpenAI raises $11B at a $1.25T valuation
items.summary: 179 points, 200 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (247wallst.com)

→ HN comments  ·  179 points  ·  200 comments

Top #1 — cmiles8:

The real headline is that they couldn’t hit what they wanted in terms of valuation and funds raised. Just were not enough people willing to invest given concerns that it may be downhill from here for a while on AI.

This will also make it even harder to avoid any future IPO being a down round. They’re almost certainly worth much less than Anthropic and Anthropic is, per reports, struggling to keep its valuation much above 1T, and even that may fall through.

↳ reply 1 — onlyrealcuzzo:

The bigger story is that their burn rate is so high.

Unless things change considerably, this is less than a 6 month runway.

It's not common for raises to give you this little runway.

You could read into it that they expect to IPO in far less than that amount of time, and this is a short bridge until then.

↳↳ reply — metalspot:

This would by my question. Why do they need money at all after just raising 9 months ago?

But none of these numbers are real. Softbank and MGX are re-arranging the deck chairs between OpenAI and Stargate so the actual new outside money here indicates very weak demand.

This is a press release to try to anchor the valuation but it doesn't seem like a lot of people are buying that.

↳ reply 2 — steelframe:

No idea who's actually worth more than who here, but I will say that recently I've stopped using Opus at work for the lion's share of technical work. I used GPT-6.1 Sol for one big project I tackled last week, where the agents spent about 20 hours to produce ~73k LoC across 22 PRs. While the technical decisions and code weren't bad and design gaps were left clearly enumerated, the overall "human factor" was terrible, in the sense that the plan docs were overly-verbose and difficult to read and PR descriptions were abysmal. Numbers and words were run together all over the place where there should have been spaces. At that point I pointed Opus 5.5 at the whole thing and asked it to double-check design and code and rewrite all the "for human consumption" text in plan docs and PR description, and it did a phenomenal job of that part of it. Plan docs were made much more concise with emphasis on the strategic parts of the problem. Opus accepted the vast majority of the design and code that GPT-6.1 Sol had produced.

Of course I have no idea what the technical results would have been if I had just used Opus 5.5 end-to-end, but I'm fairly confident it would have been more expensive given the rates my company pays for each. For that matter I wonder how Kimi3.1 Pro or DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 would have done with various parts of the job. In fact I may try rerunning the whole thing using open weight models next week just out of curiosity.

If Kimi+DeepSeek produce something roughly equivalent, then just from my own personal experience with a novel problem involving legacy in-house code, as opposed to public benchmarks for which I don't have a great handle on how well they correlate with value produced by the models, that will make me question the valuation of both OpenAI and Anthropic.

↳ reply 3 — admax88qqq:

> They’re almost certainly worth much less than Anthropic

What makes you say this?

Top #2 — bob1029:

OpenAI seems to me like they are operating with a slightly longer horizon strategy than Anthropic. Going for the IPO is the last resort in my mind. It is what you do to get ahead of deteriorating financial conditions. I don't think Anthropic had a choice at their projected burn rate. Why would we surrender all our cloaks and daggers unless we absolutely have to? The political and regulatory headwinds are not looking favorable for AI companies as of a few days ago.

Going for the IPO collapses a large space of options that are available to the business. The AI business is entirely about data. Anthropic's IPO would generate an incredible amount of data that could be used by its competitors to refine their strategy. Knowing where to allocate capital is perhaps worth more than the capital itself at these scales.

↳ reply — ozgrakkurt:

I like how nothing you are writing is based on anything. Just vibes all around, optimus robots, flying cars, bioweapons, space data centers.

Top #3 — chris_va:

We always see these headlines and think "is XYZ company actually worth that much?"

Class A stock gets paid out first, so "valuation" here is not what a retail investor would necessarily pay for class C.

Basically, do these people think that they'll get their $11B back? If so, they are ok with a high "valuation" because there is little risk. And with OpenAI's corporate structure, who knows what is actually happening.

items.title: Person of Interest
items.summary: 273 points, 180 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (krthr.co)

→ HN comments  ·  273 points  ·  180 comments

Top #1 — vesche:

From reading the comments, I think a lot of people haven’t seen the show. I highly recommend it. However, you have to remember that this aired on CBS in the age of shows like CSI and NCIS. Therefore, it was made into a high-episode-number, cookie cutter serial crime drama. Every episode follows a similar pattern where the two main characters are trying to prevent a murder. However… if you can make it past that and especially stay focused thru two seasons of that - you will be massively rewarded. The later seasons especially are essentially a fantastic, complex, hard sci-fi show about proxy wars between AGIs using human agents in a battle of control. It’s honestly one of the best shows ever and way ahead of its time

↳ reply 1 — btown:

For seasons 1-2 I highly recommend this watch/skip list: https://www.tumblr.com/abigailnussbaum/152346270515/person-o...

You lose some character moments, but you get to everything the parent post described far quicker. And it’s well, well worth it, especially for those of us working with AI.

PoI asks these incredible questions: how do you design an AGI system that can optimize for saving lives, without it taking a strictly utilitarian view that leads inexorably to it trying to take over the world?

And how do you, as a human trying to get the best of both worlds, keep yourself sane when the tradeoffs are visceral and painful and demand a sacrifice?

You get to know a group of lovable, flawed, but highly competent weirdos who are trying to muddle through this. (With Amy Acker’s incredible performance a particular highlight!)

(It’s also the source of the four-people-pointing-guns-at-each-other-in-church meme, which is delightfully lampshaded in universe.)

Highly recommend.

↳↳ reply — soraminazuki:

> PoI asks these incredible questions: how do you design an AGI system that can optimize for saving lives, without it taking a strictly utilitarian view that leads inexorably to it trying to take over the world?

I don't think the show ever addressed those questions in a meaningful way? Basically there was a "good" AI, and later in the show, an "evil" one. And that was that.

The show did show us a convincing picture of the dangers of pervasive mass surveillance paired with an autonomous system that can sift through all of that data.

↳↳↳ reply — handoflixue:

I'm surprised none of the other replies cover this:

The "Good" AI is only allowed to draw human attention to an issue - it cannot act, and the humans fundamentally have to (a) figure out what the issue even IS and (b) how to resolve it, basically entirely on their own. Humanity is fundamentally still in charge, the AI just occasionally nudges us to look in the right direction.

Conversely, the "Evil" AI is allowed to do whatever it wants - humanity is no longer in the loop.

And, indeed, the show goes further: they might very well be considered equally moral from some sort of Utilitarian 10,000-foot view. The "Evil" AI wants to save Africa from poverty and pestilence while the "Good" AI is helpless to act on that scale. The moral difference comes down almost entirely to the idea of "minimal intervention" vs "radical revolution"

↳ reply 2 — barrell:

I first saw an episode a few seasons in, I can’t remember which. It came on in the background while at a friends house and it kept distracting me. I didn’t catch the name of the show and spent years looking for it.

I actually stumbled upon Person of Interest a couple times, but the first couple episodes were so unlike what I saw I figured it was a different series.

Eventually I realized it was the same show, and was able to watch the first couple seasons with baited breath trying to figure out how it became the show in the episode that I glimpsed before… and if it even was as good as I thought it was years prior.

So maybe watch a random episode in the fourth season of you don’t like season one? XD

edit: it was even better than I remember. It became one of my favorite series, probably the one I still think about the most to this day

↳ reply 3 — mindcrime:

The later seasons especially are essentially a fantastic, complex, hard sci-fi show about proxy wars between AGIs using human agents in a battle of control. It’s honestly one of the best shows ever and way ahead of its time

100% this. And definitely incredibly relevant to contemporary times.

Top #2 — vgalin:

I often think about Person of Interest, and when I clicked on the post, I expected to be presented with something else entirely, as the show is now 15 years old. What a pleasant surprise!

I like to compare how similar or different The Machine is to current state-of-the-art LLMs. Interestingly, in this fiction, The Machine's preferred way of communicating doesn't seem to be through text, or even artificial speech. It can see almost everything, and seems capable of improving itself, but it feels "intelligent" in a way that humans or LLMs aren't. Maybe the writers thought that giving it the ability to write text or speak directly would make it "less" in many ways (less mysterious, less machine-like, less intelligent, etc.). It also gives the impression that you cannot really guess what it "thinks" or fully understand it.

I'm also realizing that most of the time, characters don't really have a "conversation" with The Machine, whereas it is a core feature of current-day LLMs. And The Machine doesn't even "create" its communication channels, it uses existing ones (phone booth, radio ...).

↳ reply — a012:

In some flashbacks the author of the machine was using a chat interface in his terminal. I think he decided to let it to be entirely machine so that’s why it didn’t have a “voice”

↳↳ reply — Izkata:

Any interface is a possible entrypoint to hack in and gain access to the machine (the government made several attempts over the course of the series, we even meet one of the hackers). Losing that chat interface was part of locking it down before handing it over to the government, so they couldn't weaponize it, and it comes back in the 5th season (not as a retcon, as circumstances within the series).

Top #3 — microflash:

Pleasantly surprised to see this here. One of the most memorable shows that I watched ages ago. It was strong at the beginning but kind of dragged on in later seasons. Still very nice to binge.

In case you’re looking for some more shows related to AI, Cupertino by Robert King and Michelle King is currently airing and is pretty entertaining.

↳ reply 1 — Bender:

It did start to drag on but I still enjoyed it even though I was only able to watch it via Amazon's FreeVee with all their weird commercials. I watched it just to see root [1].

[1] - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BN1sGIqdSUA

↳↳ reply — microflash:

Amy Acker was definitely fantastic as Root.

↳ reply 2 — ghaff:

I enjoyed it for a bit but it was one of those shows that just didn't grab me after a while. But, then, I'm like that with a lot of shows and don't really binge watch. The few times I've bought a full series which I enjoyed on DVD, I've found that I watch it some and then drift away.

items.title: Petered
items.summary: 149 points, 89 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (aworkinglibrary.com)

→ HN comments  ·  149 points  ·  89 comments

Top #1 — bloomingeek:

<“A-people hire A-people, B-people hire C-people”>

I didn't go into management because I didn't think circumstances were stable enough. I did see four co-workers go up the ladder, with disastrous results. Two of them I tried to warn, the other two would have been a waste of time to warn. By the time I retired, two had been fired, one drank himself into a coma, then passed away. The fourth is still working, but became so hated, the company keeps moving him to different posts. All four of these cases were promoted by management personnel who were "people persons", but were terrible decision makers.

There's an old saying, "Ain't nothing to it, if you're born to it." I know it's too simplistic, but it's based on a lot of reality.

Top #2 — carschno:

I think the Peter Principle addresses a good point, but misses a critical one: the hierarchy itself. Obviously, a manager requires different skills than an engineer, so why should a good engineer be a good manager? This holds the other way round: a good manager is not particularly likely to be a good engineer.

Both is fine, these are just different jobs. However, the problem is that the manager is 'above' the engineer in the generally accepted hierarchy. Consequently, engineers are pressured to become managers for the development. As long as this hierarchy exists, the problem will exist.

↳ reply 1 — mft_:

My experience in a large ‘industry’ (not IT) is that we: a) are very bad at knowing how to measure performance b) mostly only measure performance as an individual contributor, and not as a manager or leader. (Which is to say: of course managers and leaders have their performance assessed, but it is often via the same tools/questions used for individual contributors, rather than specifically measuring skills in management or leadership domains) Then you overlay this with human factors such as nepotism, conflict aversion, politics, friendships… and of course we screw it all up overall. —- So, to your point, absolutely we’re bad at selecting people who have the aptitude to be a good manager or leader for such roles, and terrible at weeding out people who aren’t suited.

↳ reply 2 — vladms:

> As long as this hierarchy exists, the problem will exist.

I would encourage you to try to setup a place where no hierarchy exists and see how it goes. In my experience people have wildly different opinions on multiple (even minor) things and without someone to "take a decision", things end up just going in circles.

Of course, if the person taking the decisions repeatedly takes decisions that have a negative longer term impact (much easier to asses on longer term than at the moment you have to take the decision), something should change, but that can include contributors looking for other companies ...

Top #3 — JSR_FDED:

After they’ve been promoted to their level of incompetence, they lean in very hard on relationships to survive.

Organizations where they get away with this are miserable to work for, and their influence ensures nothing merit-related ever happens again. Literally the source of the famous expression “A-people hire A-people, B-people hire C-people”.

↳ reply — ricardobeat:

I never thought of that quote was something connected to management. What makes you think that?

Here is it straight from the source: https://guykawasaki.com/the_art_of_recr-2/

↳↳ reply — PebblesRox:

It seems straightforwardly about management decisions to me given that it’s about who to hire.

What’s your interpretation? What do you connect it to, if not management?

items.title: Writing as a thinking tool
items.summary: 211 points, 72 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (muratbuffalo.blogspot.com)

→ HN comments  ·  211 points  ·  72 comments

Top #1 — billypilgrim:

When I had started my PhD, I thought the writing part of a paper was just the last thing I needed to do to summarize my results, like a boring epilogue to the more exciting science. What surprised me was how much of the scientific process relied on my ability to convey my ideas to someone else. And to be able to do that you need clarity of mind, you need to have worked through multiple drafts to be able to get to your point as efficiently and clearly as possible. So many times I only discovered what I was actually researching during the writing part.

The problem with AI writing is that it makes people believe that writing is just writing and not a tool for thinking very deeply about the topic you are writing about. I am not completely opposed to AI assisted writing, but if I see AI writing, it’s telling me that the author tried to take a shortcut in their own thinking and it’s a good heuristic that the ideas will not be thought through enough to warrant my complete attention.

↳ reply 1 — torben-friis:

>it’s telling me that the author tried to take a shortcut in their own thinking and it’s a good heuristic that the ideas will not be thought through enough to warrant my complete attention.

Even worse: Facing AI writing, there's a strong suspicion that any concerns or counterpoints you bring won't be actually considered, but rather copypasted into an llm session.

↳↳ reply — sublinear:

That's a good thing. The writer who has nothing to say and the dumb audience who doesn't care stay down where they belong pacified by their "AI".

↳ reply 2 — cameldrv:

Same with reading actually. Reading a book makes you think for a long time about the subject and form your own judgments. I like audiobooks and online content too, but they don’t seem to stimulate this nearly as much.

For audiobooks, I seem to not have as much of a tendency to pause the audio and stop and think, and it’s harder to reread a passage, so it’s a more passive experience.

For online content, there’s not as much of an intention to fully engage with the material. It’s easy to skim or switch to something else.

↳ reply 3 — bartread:

The trick, I think - at least this has helped me - is not to use the AI to write for me, nor to use it to rewrite my drafts, but is to do the writing myself and to ask it for editorial feedback. This forces me to think through what I’ve written more deeply, and then rewrite it according to that deeper understanding.

I think if I used AI for the actual writing then, (a) there’d be a lot missing, and (b) I’d rob myself of much of the value, in better understanding, of writing myself.

We’re not all the same so YMMV, but this is what I’ve found from using AI in various ways to see if and how it can help with writing.

Top #2 — drewbeck:

This is true for designing, too. I see a lot of people saying Figma is dead because you can prototype directly; for novel UX problems the act of designing — of putting ideas together, assembling a component, even getting good data into a design — is where a lot of my thinking and insights develop. The brain work plus the craft work, the tight loop between thinking and creating is so critical for me and I haven’t found nearly the same feeling when prompting.

In writing and designing I think we often have a thought-feeling first: something inchoate that we can’t quite articulate yet. Getting directly to the medium itself — text or frames and layouts — is how we give shape to that feeling and turn it into a concept, insight or design.

↳ reply 1 — gobdovan:

I actually appreciate working with LLMs on design quite a lot, although I'm not a designer by trade so my situation may differ. I enjoy getting an image-generated mockup (that is usually top class), then letting an LLM implement it, then seeing where it doesn't feel quite right. Then trying to understand why it doesn't feel right. When I do the CSS myself, I iterate one component at a time and usually not get the 'find the 100 differences' feel. Animations are even more fun, you feel they suck, but you have to slow them down to understand what's really making them suck. Not claiming I can do good designs, but it helped me identify faster why some designs were bad.

↳ reply 2 — levmiseri:

I see what you are saying and for very specific problems/explorations I do still reach for Figma. But the days of crafting static screens and multi-artboard flows are gone. It's better to prototype the entire flow/interaction directly than trying to reason about it 'statically'. LLMs have also opened up an entire array of new possibilities for e.g. combining meaningful 3D and taking a 'leap of faith' into visualizations/interactions that would simply be too costly to properly explore before

Top #3 — urda:

I always carry a small Moleskine notebook, the pocket-sized hardcover with grid paper, for notes, thoughts, and whatever else comes to mind during the day. Each page is numbered, and I continue the numbering as I move from one notebook to the next. This allows quick reference to past ideas, thoughts, or notes I may have in an older notebook, or even a few pages back. It is the primary way I get thoughts to paper, and is the "entry point" to all my writing and thinking.

Notebooks do not crash, do not freeze, and need only you and a pen. My notebooks often remind me of this passage from "Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance":

> “For this you keep a lab notebook. Everything gets written down, formally, so that you know at all times where you are, where you’ve been, where you’re going and where you want to get. In scientific work and electronics technology this is necessary because otherwise the problems get so complex you get lost in them and confused and forget what you know and what you don’t know and have to give up.”

> Robert M. Pirsig, Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance

items.title: Llama-modchip: 284B DeepSeek on 64GB RAM, no GPU
items.summary: 299 points, 113 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  299 points  ·  113 comments

Top #1 — kennywinker:

The floor for a functional local AI system keeps getting lower, dispite ram and GPU prices continuing to go up. An E5 workstation with lots of threads, $300 of RAM and at least $100 of GPU gets you something that can do >100tok/s+ prompt processing, and ~20tok/s output with Qwen3.8-flash-next:IQ3_S. Toss a $500 GPU in there, and it goes from barely usable to pleasingly performant. For less than $800 you have something that holds its own with where the SOTA was less than a year ago.

I don't see how anyone justifies a claude subscription. Do you want to rent the tools you use to making a living from the people who are trying to automate away your job?

↳ reply 1 — eddyg:

Because retail models now dominate the price-performance frontier by a huge margin. An open-weight model wins at just 3% of price points (down from 41% just a few months ago).

https://village.dev/blog/closed-ai-models-now-dominate-the-p...

↳↳ reply — kennywinker:

That chart is comparing the cost of buying tokens, not the cost of generating your own. The system I specced out can generate 5.2M tokens per day.

That's $104/day of opus 5.5 tokens, or $265/day of fable 5.1 tokens.

If you were able to saturate usage of this system, you could pay it off in 3 days of fable time or 6 days of opus 5.5.

But ok those are more intelligent. Let's go with something that scores similar - sonnet 4.6. 5.2M tokens is $78/day and the system is paid off in 8 days.

↳↳↳ reply — discordance:

Are you considering intelligence per token?

1 qwen output token != 1 opus output token.

↳ reply 2 — gavinray:

Comparing the sort of models that would run on that to frontier models like Opus 5.5 or Astra is silly

↳ reply 3 — monocasa:

It is weirdly inverted from the previously standard economics where hardware would keep getting cheaper but those efficiency gains would keep at least partially eaten by software.

Top #2 — armcat:

Something to keep in mind with aggressive quantisation, is that it's been empirically proven [1] that (1) quantisation has non-linear performance behaviour, and (2) generally the peak size-to-performance ratio occurs at 4-bit; anything lower and you will see significant reduction in performance.

Also, I've been playing with speech models for the past 2 years, and for me anything below 8-bit is a huge drop in quality; so quantisation for LLMs and for other bespoke modality models, is not 1:1.

[1] "Reliability Scaling Laws for Quantized Large Language Models", TUM, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.10855

↳ reply 1 — Youden:

I think your leading statement is a bit more authoritative than what the linked paper actually demonstrates. It demonstrates your claimed qualities for specific algorithms, methodologies, and models.

It explicitly says that Quantization-Aware Training is out of scope, may reveal different trends and has potential for extreme quantization. Heavily-quantized model releases today generally use QAT or something similar, so I don't think the paper can be universally applied to modern quants (e.g. [0]).

That said, I don't see any evidence that TFA does any of that so the paper's claims may be quite applicable there.

[0]: https://huggingface.co/vcruz305/DSV4.1-Flash-1017-SAGE-REXL3...

↳↳ reply — fho:

I recently did some toying around with (very) small language models (<200k). I used QAT from the beginning and was surprised that I got byte identical results from the int8 model vs the float32 one.

If that scales with parameters I don't see why QAT shouldn't be the norm.

(As I was only comparing the QAT f32 model vs the quantization its possible that a not QAT f32 would have performed even better)

↳↳↳ reply — lostmsu:

Do you think QAT isn't the norm yet?

I expected it to be the norm since GPT-OSS

↳ reply 2 — onlyrealcuzzo:

I imagine that it's just the non-linearity of audio makes it easily apparent how much quantization really matters, and that benchmaxxing is so ingrained in LLMs that if you simply run them through benchmarks, they can do well under quantization, when in reality, they have a similar drop off that they do in audio, it just doesn't slam you in the face at every turn as obviously.

Top #3 — aappleby:

Stupid question, but does this AI-generated repo actually _do_ anything?

Comparing it on Nemotron, it runs just about the same as plain old llama.cpp on the cpu (except prefill seems much faster). I don't see an option to set up DeepSeek in "modchip setup", so I haven't tested that one yet.

Edit: this is on a Ryzen 7945hx 16-core Zen 4 + 96 gb DDR5.

↳ reply — ar-nelson:

Yeah, I was wondering the same thing. I thought about trying to run DeepSeek v4 on my old-but-still-pretty-fast Intel Xeon server with 24 cores and 96GB of DDR4. The "check CPU readiness" script called it "Tier A", so I was optimistic. The default `modchip` app just installs Nemotron and says nothing about DeepSeek. Following the instructions to install their quant of DeepSeek, running it with `modchip start` fails with:

> llama_model_load: error loading model: check_tensor_dims: tensor 'blk.0.ffn_gate_tid2eid.weight' has wrong shape; expected 4, 129280, got 6, 129280, 1, 1

And running the bundled llama-cpp instance from the download, as shown in the readme, fails with "Illegal instruction (core dumped)". So I have no idea how to run this.

items.title: Agent memory needs its OpenTelemetry moment
items.summary: 155 points, 101 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (lorekit.io)

→ HN comments  ·  155 points  ·  101 comments

Top #1 — armchairhacker:

Is this a significant problem? It seems like there are 15 solutions to every AI “text format” problem, but all are merely structure over feeding the AI informal English, structure which I believe the “transformer” model is specifically able to strip to a common form (which is how training it on the entire internet worked).

AI does benefit from learning to use skills, and being instructed with good structures (like “save [specific important kind of detail] in memories” and “plan before implementing anything”). But none of these memory solutions seem better than any other, they’re basically just different folders. Your CLAUDE.md can say “see AGENTS.md” and AGENTS.md can say “write memories to .agent/memories/“, and I’d be interested in a measurement, but I assume it performs almost the exact same as native CLAUDE.md and .claude/memories.

One thing I’ve noticed AI does much better than me, is not have OCD over the “perfect” solution.

↳ reply 1 — bee_rider:

As someone not involved in AI development, it seems really surprising that memories are another text-format issue. Seems like (in a human analogy) something more equivalent to your notebook or scratchpad.

Memories are lossy things that live in our brains, I’d expect they to be stored in some native LLM encoded representation (which would make the lack of standardization understandable).

This probably seems like a dumb distinction, but I think some of the problems in the article come from calling these things memories. Like, the prompt injection/provenience issue. The model has received some notes from someone about a topic, if it they were treated as “notes from <whoever sent them> about <topic>” instead of “my memories about <topic>” that should put things on the right footing to start at least, right?

↳↳ reply — wongarsu:

The issue with storing the memories in some encoded representation (e.g. in embedding space) is that this would turn that representation into something that has to be supported "forever". I have projects that I have worked on with Opus 4.6, 4.7, 4.8, 5, 5.5, as well as Fable 5 and 5.1, and obvious some Sonnet subagents along the way. And I expect to keep working on the same codebase when Opus 6 and Opus 7 release. Text is trivially compatible with all of those, but their embeddings all differ. And whatever other representation you come up with right now in Opus 5.5 might no longer make sense in the model architecture of Opus 7

Imho the interesting challenges with memory are about "what does this memory belong to" (attaching it to lines of code or similar), "what does it relate to" (webs of memories), "is this even still true" ("sleeping", "reconciliation", etc). But there's no real consensus what is even useful to handle, never mind how to handle it

↳ reply 2 — reactordev:

This is what happens when you treat the LLM as a black box, you end up building the same stuff around it. Like trying to make your dog understand your intentions. You can train it to do tricks and it recognizes specific reward patterns but most dogs have no idea what you’re saying beyond basic triggers.

Top #2 — speedping:

Entire blog post reeks of LLM. If there was an adequately reliable way of detecting LLM text i'd build a browser extension that would just filter it out altogether.

↳ reply 1 — jaynate:

Thought the same thing and was surprised how high this was ranking. I wonder if we are starting to look past the LLM stank and into the core of the idea (which is solid in this case)? If HN, a highly discerning crowd, is able to look past it then many other audiences are probably okay with it too

↳↳ reply — grey-area:

Often people don't even read the article, they just see a headline they agree with and upvote it.

I usually read the comments before deciding if the article is worth my time.

↳ reply 2 — ulrikrasmussen:

Exactly, and LLMs cannot describe architectures, period. On the surface it looks coherent, but everything is vague and lacks rigor. Instead of defining concepts and giving them a name, LLMs keep referring to them using vague terms such as "address and key is where the memory is true". What the fuck does that mean? Give each concept a name and explain them.

This has no value because noone can separate what was designed by a human from design details that the LLM made up on the spot. That's fine for one-off generated stuff like web pages, but as a proposed standard for everyone to build on? No.

Top #3 — Fordec:

On the general premise, I agree. But I don't think that moment is today, not yet anyway. I don't think we understand the right way to approach context and memory yet or how long they should last for, never mind standardizing on an abstraction prematurely that ends up being like SOAP or SGML.

↳ reply 1 — andai:

What's better than SGML? What would XML an HTML look like if they were based on that instead?

↳↳ reply — moron4hire:

HTML is SGML. You know that while doctype things you're supposed to out at the start of the document? That specifies the document schema of HTML at a specific version for the current SGML doc.

↳↳↳ reply — andai:

Yeah, hence my question. What would HTML and XML look like if they were based on this thing that's apparently superior to SGML instead of being based on SGML?

↳ reply 2 — dizhn:

Fully agree. Any solution people think they have today is working on assumptions that are probably not correct. And things are still moving very fast.

Top #1 — bcherny:

Boris from the Claude Code team here. Historically Claude Code has not done secret scrubbing (there are many good tools for that), but we are looking into what we can do to prevent this.

That said, a few thoughts:

1. .claude/settings.local.json is meant to stay local. This is not a file you should check into source control. We automatically gitignore it when Claude creates the file, so in this case the files were manually created and checked in (docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings)

2. Permission rules are old hat. Everyone should be using auto mode instead. It is safer and also does not require manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists. Auto mode is enabled by default and is included for free in all plans.

3. Regardless of what agent you use, you should have secret scanning enabled. GitHub and other source control hosts offer it. There are many threat models that it protects against and you should absolutely use it if you can. (see https://github.com/security/plans)

↳ reply 1 — futhey:

I'm not here to be critical, but the hoops you have to jump through to get Claude out of .env is more than it should be. You basically need an agent to write it if it's anything complicated, like, allow .env.example but not .env.*.

Whereas that should probably be default on instead, and this should apply to other known sensitive folders. A simpler system like .agentignore would be even better.

I like auto mode but "the agent supervises itself" is a bad compliance/safety answer on its own.

↳ reply 2 — eddy162:

Saying the answer is auto mode almost feels insulting as a developer. Claude loves showing me the most obscure bash commands where it hides its edits to numerous files and runs who knows what that there's barely a time where I don't have to ask it to use edit mode and to show human-readable bash commands. Using Claude has become a fight in maintaining control over how my codebase works so that I'm not dependent on Claude to do literally anything.

↳ reply 3 — markasoftware:

Auto mode cannot be considered safer than anything because it does not even attempt to guarantee any sort of security. The threat model is not even defined. It cannot be quantified or compared with any other approach other than "full access"

Top #2 — Aurornis:

Confusing headline. They scanned for repos where people had committed their .claude/ folder and local settings and then scanned those files for commands which contained keys or passwords.

So pressing “Don’t Ask Again” by itself doesn’t expose passwords by itself. If you commit your local Claude settings and in those settings you have manually approved commands containing secrets directly in the command and then you publish the repo, that’s exposed.

Top #3 — tsergiu:

I'm super paranoid about the level of access AI agents have. At the same time, I want them to take away the tedium of a bunch of tasks I'm required to do, and it sucks to have to micromanage them.

The best solution I've been able to come up is using an ephemeral vm (on an isolated network) per task, using --dangerously-skip-permissions so it doesn't bother me. I couple that with an API proxy that lets me restrict the permissions it has to external services. So e.g. where a quickbooks API key gives the holder "god mode" access, the proxy lets the agent do certain read commands without confirmation, but all write endpoints except uploading receipts require confirmation on my phone before they'll be allowed to hit the quickbooks servers. I no longer need to trust that the agent will interpret my readonly wishes correctly.

Tooting my own horn here, but this setup works incredibly well! I've been able to connect dozens of services safely where I absolutely do not trust giving raw, overpowered credentials or oauth integration to the agent directly. I actually just released the API proxy today at https://keycontain.com

items.title: The end of Microsoft Research's AI Frontiers group
items.summary: 394 points, 230 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (hunch.net)

→ HN comments  ·  394 points  ·  230 comments

Top #1 — AnotherGoodName:

This is true in every large company right now.

The transformer based approach is seen as a highway to race down in terms of training and building better models with minimal organizational distractions allowed while every company puts its foot down on this highway. Exploratory research into other AI methods is highly discouraged for now and organizations are encouraging transformer based scale out and iteration as a top priority.

As an example Meta literally fired it's previously head of AI who held views that transformers won't scale. He wanted to veer off the highway and heavily fund exploratory new types of models. They got someone willing to scale the current method out. Essentially the messaging it "Foot down, there's a straight highway ahead don't divert".

I have the view this makes sense too. Current top models are mere (mere in big datacenter terms) trillions of parameters right now. We definitely haven't hit the ceiling and everyone's noticing "Hey this Opus 5.5 with the increased parameters seems much better than the last one". Well that's a trillion parameter model. We'll soon start hitting 10's of trillions and 100's of trillions of parameter models. Unless there's a ceiling which nobody expects they should keep scaling just as they have been. I really do agree that it'd be insane to veer off this highway with exploratory research at this particular point in time. Foot down, get to 10 trillion parameters, see if the scaling holds, if so off to 100 trillion parameters. If the scaling continues to hold we'll be asking the AI to do the exploratory research for us soon enough.

↳ reply 1 — redox99:

> As an example Meta literally fired it's previously head of AI who held views that transformers won't scale. He wanted to veer off the highway and heavily fund exploratory new types of models.

Almost all statements Yann LeCun made back then (LLMs won't be able to do this or that) turned out to be wrong. They were right to fire him.

↳↳ reply — Animats:

Historically, that happens now and then. Examples include color television cameras and fluorescent lamp ballasts.

RCA developed the first good color TV cameras. They were monsters. Originally, electronic TV (as opposed to mechanical scanning) used Zworykin's iconoscope. This needed huge amounts of light. It didn't have a photo-multiplier stage to boost sensitivity, but it did accumulate charge from light over the whole frame time. There was an alternative approach, Farnsworth's image dissector, which also needed huge amounts of light. It had a photo-multiplier stage but only the light from the dot currently being scanned by the scanning beam mattered.

So RCA threw money at the problem. They developed the image orthicon camera tube. It combined the advantages of both approaches, integration over a full frame and a photo-multiplier stage. It was insanely expensive, costing thousands of dollars in the 1950s. It needed about twenty different voltages and multiple independent power supplies. It worked reasonably well.

Then came color. That took three image orthicons (RGB) inside a box the size of a small refrigerator, along with optics to split the incoming image into three colors. Plus a rack of analog electronics per camera, connected through a large cable. Plus an alignment problem from hell, with a huge number of adjustment knobs.[1]

Scaling worked! From the 1950s to the 1970s, color TV broadcasting was powered by those monsters.

Now, independent of this, other people were working on other approaches. Vidicons, silicon detectors inside camera tubes, and finally fully solid state image sensors. Eventually, in 1983, after thirty years of image orthicon monsters, RCA produced a usable solid state camera. Today, a cell phone camera costs about US$10 in bulk, and it's far better than the monsters.

It took thirty years of low-priority development to get past the giant image orthicon cameras.

Electronic fluorescent lamp ballasts had a different problem. That was a suppressed invention. The magnetic ballast industry was dominated by Magnetek. Someone invented a solid state replacement, which was smaller and cheaper, and licensed their patent to Magnetek for royalties. Magnetek just sat on it, not wanting to gut their core market. The inventor hired Townsend, Townsend and Crew in Palo Alto and sued. (Read this in the law firm's brag book in their office.) Eventually, the inventor got a hundred million or so, solid state ballasts went into production, and Magnetek seems to be gone. (The company called Magnetek today, which makes crane controls, is an offshoot of a Litton unit, and seems to be unrelated.)

There are also parallels from the steam locomotive industry, the Baldwin Locomotive Works being the best known. Baldwin actually built the first Diesel locomotive. They made a few half-hearted tries at Diesels over several decades, then gave up and went back to steam. Baldwin ceased all locomotive production in 1956. The corporation lingered on for a while, not doing much.

[1] https://www.tvcameramuseum.org/rca/tk40a/pix/rcatk40aart.pdf

items.title: MaxxBench – "Nice DeepSWE score. But is it true?"
items.summary: 206 points, 63 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (maxxbench.unlap.ai)

→ HN comments  ·  206 points  ·  63 comments

Top #1 — kqr:

This is a great example of how to test how well a benchmark score generalises. The first order approximation is not complicated: just vary a parameter and see how much the score changes.

Which parameter to vary depends on the result of the test, but the MaxxBench route of varying the task spec seems like a good default, though not always the most informative.

In one of my private benchmarks I realised many of the less capable models didn't fail because they submitted the wrong answer, but because they exceeded their budget for number of tool calls they were allowed. The more capable models never got close to the tool call limit because they tended toward combining tool calls (e.g. chaining multiple shell commands in one Bash tool call).

Was my benchmark actually measuring ability to combine tool calls rather than reasoning ability on the problem at hand? Well, easy enough to find out: re-run under a different tool call budget and see how much the scores change.

(Next problem: is ability to combine tool calls a useful thing to measure, i.e. should it confer an advantage in the benchmark? It could be if it is a sign of planning multiple steps ahead.)

Top #2 — kqr:

I'm surprised by four things:

(1) An established framework for model evaluation runs the inference call with API key inside the isolated envionment the agent harness has full access to. Especially when it's intended to be an offline environment, that seems kinda... dumb. The language model itself is not dangerous -- it's only text. Inference is fine to do outside the isolated environment. It's only the harness' tools that can have effects on the enironment, so those need to be sent to the sandbox.

(2) Only a small set of language models exploited this! I run private benchmarks a lot and I know how much the language models try to anticipate grader behaviour when the task is bechmark-shaped. I would have thought more of them would request the answer from the web.

(3) It takes someone else to mutate the task specification. When I'm looking at an older iteration of one of my private benchmarks, the first thing I do is add a small twist to it to see how much of a passing grade is learned/anticipated. Seems like a cheap and easy coalmine canary that's in the interest of the evaluator.

(4) MaxxBench did not try to dress some DeepSWE tasks in clothes that make them look less benchmarky. Their purpose seems to be answering "how well does DeepSWE enchmark scores generalise?" Part of the generalisation error is memorised solutions, yes, but another part is that models emit different behaviour when they suspect they are in a benchmark. By being careful to not leak the benchmark nature of the task, models spend a lot less time reasoning about the behaviour of the grader and this is likely to produce different performance on the mutated task. It would be interesting to know in what direction that effect points, because that is the performance people get out of the model in real situations. (In my experience, hiding the benchmark nature of the task can produce improved performance on both the original and the mutated task, but particularly the latter.)

↳ reply — rbehrends:

> I run private benchmarks a lot and I know how much the language models try to anticipate grader behaviour when the task is bechmark-shaped. I would have thought more of them would request the answer from the web.

This is something I was thinking about, too. More than once I've observed a model note in a reasoning trace something along the lines of "this looks like a coding test" (could possibly also refer to leetcode style problems, but same difference). Models often also seem to behave differently in response to one-shot prompts.

On occasions where I let a model do autonomous work, I usually don't just give it a prompt for this reason. I write a CONCEPT.md file, then refine that interactively into a SPEC.md file to find and resolve ambitaskguities (and possibly also create an ARCHITECTURE.md file, if it isn't a one-off ). At this point, most models seem to no longer see it as a benchmark or competitive programming problem, but a proper software engineering task and are less prone to reward hacking (with the caveat that these are very subjective and unfalsifiable impressions).

Top #3 — antirez:

I bet we will find this is mostly that smaller models have issues to go against: 1. strong priors that are inverted here in the changes of the benchmarks. 2. underspecified specs for which hidden tests test things not clearly stated, but that very large models can guess knowing they are tested.

To the shocking number of people here who are justifying this or explaining how it only affect swipe input as if that makes it better: soft coercion is still coercion. If I made a physical keyboard that stops keys from working when you're about to finish typing something I don't want you to type, but you can still circumvent it, I still made a censorship keyboard. ↳ reply 1 — Arnt:

I wrote something like this a long time ago. The customer's request was: "don't make this software produce swear words on its own". Note: on its own.

Producing "trump is …" when a user wants that is one thing. Producing that when the user wants something else could be construed as coming from the software itself, and we all know that people looking for a shitstorm will seize the opportunity.

So probabilistic software like a swipe interpreter will often be written to avoid some guesses, to lessen the chance of a shitstorm. Users who want that output have to use a dependable input method instead of one based on probabilities and guesswork.

IMO this avoidance isn't among the ten worst consequences of shitstorms.

↳↳ reply — scratcheee:

An even more generous interpretation (not saying this is the case and a complete excuse, but might explain some of the choices) is that there are some phrases people do not want to type by accident.

Top #3 — schiffern:

One thing about panspermia math: why assume current travel conditions between the stars?

Today the Sun is very far from other stars, but early in star formation (within nebula) the stars are

1. much closer together

2. have a higher rate of material ejection (mass exchange)

3. likely have more benign radiation environments unless near a star, due to GCR shielding by nebula gas

4. likely have higher equilibrium temperature in interstellar/interplanetary space

Combined, these factors yield orders of magnitude improvement in panspermia efficiency vs the Sun.

↳ reply 1 — idlewords:

This has occurred to people! But if you run the numbers, they are still not good enough in that early (~100 My) window when stars in the parent nebula are close together, you get something like 1 chance in 1000 of possible panspermia events (based on modeling lumps of rock flying back and forth). Not terrible odds, but nothing like the Mars -> Earth odds.

↳↳ reply — w1:

A more extreme version of this is the idea of panspermia in the early universe, when the cosmic microwave background radiation was warm enough to keep water liquid: https://lweb.cfa.harvard.edu/~loeb/habitable.pdf

Yes indeed, I've thought panspermia in the Sun's natal cluster is an interesting idea. It would make a fine science fictional scenario that could get around the Fermi problem: those 10,000 or so systems could have life, but the rest of the universe not have life.

> "That almost nobody has the skills these days to implement something like TP is something we could eventually come to regret – or, rather, our grandchildren could. Software development is becoming a semi-skilled industry, and I doubt that the rise of AI will entirely compensate for this."

I agree, but AI also there is hope!

For many years I've worried about the ever-growing depth of abstraction in computing. There are few alive now who actually understand all of the layers on abstraction involved in modern computing, and who can debug the truly strange edge case bugs and vulnerabilities introduced by the interoperation of these many complex layers.

For a time I imagined it to be an unsolvable problem, and that there would always be only a special class of neurodivergent hyper-specialists who still mostly had to work in large teams to even come close to understanding a stack in full. We're reaching the point where a single human lifespan just isn't enough to learn it all, even for those of us with what Dilbert called "The Knack". By the time you're proficient in all of it - you're dead.

Now there is a new kind of intelligence. One that CAN fit it all in a single mind, and one that will outlive us all and continue to learn long after our meat has gone bad.

As long as the AI's stay aligned, and we find ways to build them more efficiently there's a non-zero chance that they actually make it all better instead of worse. Genuinely long-term planning and the ability to TRULY grasp the full stack COULD actually happen. At least if we use these new systems in service of the greater good, and not just to play silly games on the stock market.

items.title: Every Windows 11 app should kill Electron, and Discord just showed why
items.summary: 164 points, 173 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (windowslatest.com)

Top #1 — cheschire:

I'm pretty sure this was known since the early days of Electron. It was even one of the chief complaints about VS Code when it was first launched.

Electron's value prop has always been about having one team producing one app that is supported on multiple platforms with minimal additional effort.

This article does nothing to address that.

↳ reply 1 — accurrent:

A huge pain of desktop development is managing dependencies particularly if you are coming from C++/Native code. Imagine you wanted to make a simple app in the 2010s that accesses the webcam for instance: If you use chrome you got the full html5 runtime, whereas with other tools you'd need bespoke libraries which your end user may not have.

The only way to ship the same code between linux, macOS, and Windows would have been to either use something like Qt or the JVM back in the 2010s. The JVM desktop stuff was super ugly and Java itself had become notorious (also if you wanted anything remotely interesting like webcam/microphone or multimedia access you'd still have to ship dynamic libraries). Qt required special packaging skills to ship to the end user especially if third party libraries were involved. Electron killed that by bundling chrome (and chrome has a huge api surface).

Today, I would argue the package management situation for a language like rust is a lot different. You dont have to cobble different DLLs together, you can just statically compile dependencies and cargo/rust do a pretty good job of making sure it's bundled with your app. Other languages also now have similarly useful tools.

↳↳ reply — 72deluxe:

But then the C++ libraries you mentioned also had the ability to statically link into a binary, which means you could statically link the webcam access in, in your example. So I don't see the advantage you're arguing for?

↳↳↳ reply — cogman10:

It comes down to package distribution.

Chrome had already solved the hard problem of "how do we support webcams on linux, windows, and mac" and you as the dev just needed to use the Javascript webcam api. ( https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaDevice... )

In C++ land, you are ultimately going to either need to cook up your own webcam library or look for a 3rd party (which, in 2010, likely didn't exist) to provide it.

Today, there are a few easy to discover rust crates which provide cross platform webcam apis. But further, rust does cross platform better than C/C++ IMO. It's really easy to change how code is compiled based on the target. That was all well thought out because rust was supposed to be a language for browsers.

↳ reply 2 — ajross:

Exactly. This Discord Windows 11 rust app doesn't run on Mint or AOSP or an iPad and won't without extensive porting.

That can be done. It can be done well. It's not (or rather never has been) cheap or flexible or agile (in the market, not SWE sense). People love HTML/CSS/JS for very good reasons, and have been willing to accept the resulting tradeoffs.

Maybe that's changing now that you can vibe-port a lot of this stuff. We'll see.

↳ reply 3 — tekla:

The problem is that it made everyone's life worse.

Top #2 — EddieRingle:

Discord isn't really the model to follow here, IMO. They killed their native Android app and moved to React Native, and now they're dropping React Native (while mobile somehow keeps "native UI", according to their CTO's tweet). If they wanted to maximize code reuse and accelerate feature development, they should have instead considered Kotlin Multiplatform, then they could've skipped the React Native detour while actually building apps that are native to the platform. (Rust and its cacophony of UI frameworks are not really platform-native anywhere, as far as I'm aware. Maybe Pop OS, but I don't know anyone targeting that specifically.)

This bit is obviously subjective, but Rust as a language is simply not ergonomic enough for a lot of the use cases people are trying to apply it to, especially UI development. Most of the Rust UI libraries I've seen to date either use a more imperative style, or attempt to replicate more declarative approaches like Compose UI or SwiftUI, but without the nice language aesthetics that make it simple to read and write. And if the counter-argument there is for LLMs to be reading and writing this stuff, that's a whole other can of worms: (1) The subsidized inference era is quickly coming to an end and (2) if you're using LLMs anyway, why not maintain apps that are as native to each platform as possible?

Top #3 — LaurensBER:

Electron is pretty awesome in that it allows a small team to build a decent GUI app using their existing web skillset but it also feels like it's time for something better at this point.

With the ram prices as crazy as they are. It's pretty frustrating to have to run multiple GB eating applications just to do some basic tasks (90% is read and write messages, in the case of Discord). I understand that other people might use the more advanced features (voice chat, etc) but these could be loaded on-demand.

It's a bit crazy to me that I can comfortable run an entire Linux stack (+ Podman, monitoring, alerting and multiple services) in 512 MB ram (with 40% free, just checked!). However my Windows PC needs 5.5GB just to show the desktop! Realistically it needs somewhere between 8GB and 16GB for some basic web browsing and even then it can feel slow if you have a few apps like Discord running in the background.

↳ reply — pasc1878:

Sorry can you show a decent GUI app in Electron compared with a native one.

You show this by all your other comments on memory. The reason apps take memory is Electron.

Plus I prefer apps that behave like OS native apps not the reduced GUI of web apps.

↳↳ reply — Peanuts99:

VS Code is a perfectly fine and pretty performant app.

↳↳↳ reply — afdbcreid:

It has seen (major) optimization work, and it's still quite memory-heavy, although that's probably fine for a rich IDE. But it's not fine for many other apps.

Top #1 — thomascountz:

At one point in my life, I would've found this data fascinating (if it were opt-in, perhaps)! Now, I find it exhausting.

A similar discussion came up recently with Siri Recap[1], where some expressed how useful they thought it was and that, as a party to the conversations it summarizes, there was very little moral or ethical concern. But I have a social concern.

If I'm having a chat with someone, there's a milieu constructed around the fact that not everything will be remembered verbatim. There are all sorts of social and contextual cues that can easily get lost if listening gets replaced by flat relentless transcription.

With Recaps and this social graph (were it to be productized), the informal fluidity in the way we relate to one another starts to go away, and the expectations that follow from that become artificial and burdensome. In the same way that autocorrect has made typos unacceptable, how could you ever be forgiven for forgetting the name of your colleague's new nephew or the Italian village that your neighbor took a spontaneous boat trip to while on vacation last year?

Top #1 — tristanj:

I believe this conclusion is flawed. The author argues:

1) Unitree robots are largely made by hand.

2) Labor is approximately 8% of cost of manufacturing these robots. Because these costs are not prohibitive, there is little incentive to automate.

3) Labor costs are higher in America.

4) Therefore, American companies have higher incentive to automate.

5) Therefore, the West will capture most of the robotics opportunity.

Arguments 1-4 are reasonable, but 5 is a non-sequitur. Higher incentive to automate does not imply a better ability to automate & scale manufacturing.

I believe Unitree is currently assembling robots by hand for practical reasons:

1) Labor is still relatively cheap.

2) Humanoids and robots are evolving rapidly, changing every few months.

3) Custom assembly lines are expensive, and become obsolete when the product changes. It's difficult to maintain an assembly line when the product is rapidly evolving.

4) Tooling is inadequate. Some robotic parts are delicate, complicated, and difficult to automate manufacturing of. American companies have hit the exact same problem: Tesla is assembling the hand/forearm of Optimus by hand because it hasn't figured out how to automate manufacturing them. https://www.theverge.com/tech/1016492/tesla-optimus-robots-p... . Apparently, Tesla has hundreds of handless Optimus robots just standing around, waiting for hand manufacturing to catch up.

5) Demand is still relatively niche, these are not mass market products. Unitree only sold 5,500 robots last year. There is not enough demand to justify massive automated lines.

The author also ignores the biggest counterpoint: the Chinese have already demonstrated mastery in automated manufacturing, and have proven they can run dark factories (factories without humans) at a better scale than the west.

When humanoid robots become a mass market product (they are not ready today because the software side is majorly lacking), Chinese manufacturers are in an excellent position to rapidly automate.

Top #1 — plaidfuji:

As somebody who does ML research, LLMs certainly make ML research faster. Maybe even 10x in some cases, as the author suggests.

But that’s just the parts of ML research that take place within your compute environment, namely experiments on model architecture, training strategy, UI/UX, etc. The algorithms and software.

Just because that part of research is progressively accelerated does not imply that we’re on a collision course with world-ending “superintelligence”. It just means that you’ll get to the best possible model of your data faster. And even when your data is the entire corpus of textual knowledge, there is a limit to the utility that provides.

It just means that software engineering, data analysis, and other computational tasks will be less of a bottleneck in the overall progress of the world (which, by the way, is great, and extremely valuable).

I don’t think it’s a stretch to say that we’ll have reached max LLM capability within a couple of years (what the author refers to as “super intelligence”). But it is a huge logical leap to say this:

> If we go through this feedback loop, I expect that the AI systems that come out the other side will be able to very quickly develop novel weapons and very easily overpower human civilization in a conflict.

First of all, the weapons necessary to overpower human civilization exist. They aren’t used as such due to geopolitics and humans’ basic survival instinct. Second, developing novel weapons requires physical tests, which are decidedly not accelerated by LLMs.

AI is a tool wielded by humans. If we’re wiped out by AI, it will be at the direction of a human. But we’ve made it pretty far with some pretty unstable humans in command of planet-killer weapons. I’m not overly concerned.

Let's also imagine for the purpose of conversation that one of the things that can be gotten at an extremely high skill level through increased intelligence is the power of persuasion.

A "superintelligence" persuades humans to perform weapons tests and then to give it the ability to use the weapon.

I think everything you've said is reasonable except the bit where you think step one of an "AI" exterminating humanity wouldn't look like a human doing it. The first option doesn't to promise exponential increases whereas the second one seems to. Notably, neither the statistics nor the anecdotes we read here point to the second option.

2) Is super-intelligence something that - in control of people or out of control of people - poses a threat to humanity? That's a huge question but it seems like something deserving thought today. ↳ reply 3 — kragen:

It's worth pointing out that the humans do not have planet-killer weapons, not even biosphere-killing weapons. They could destroy civilization, but not the planet or even the species. You can make straightforward calculations showing that we already know how to build such weapons, but we haven't.

As for tools, alcohol, tobacco, fentanyl, pornography, monotheism, warfare, gambling, and money itself are "tools wielded by humans", but they still seem to get into a lot of trouble where it seems like the humans are the ones being "wielded" by the tool. And neither monotheism nor gambling is smart enough to write a compiler for me, much less choose persuasive tactics according to my personality type. A lot of humans' basic survival instinct seems to fail or even work backwards in the presence of these "tools".

Top #2 — chr15m:

Every dot in these graphs is composed of multiple benchmarks smooshed together.

Benchmarks are by definition a curated set of things that can be measured and evaluated.

Things that can be measured and evaluated can be (expensively) trained on.

The progress we are observing comes from figuring out how to measure and evaluate particular aspects of intelligence, and then expensively training on feedback loops made of those exact measurements, and synthesized data representing further measurements (literally benchmaxing).

What is not shown in these graphs are the set of things that intelligence can do, which are difficult, expensive or impossible to measure and evaluate.

That set of things is much larger than the set of benchmarks represented in the graph.

Therefore the post is misleading in the sense that the "superintelligence" being targeted is "jagged" to use Karpathy's term, and we infact already have jagged superintelligence (calculators, compilers, Bayesian spam classifiers, etc.)

We are witnessing a profound explosion of much more jagged superintelligence, restricted to the exact domains that can be (expensively) RL'ed on.

> The configuration used here had no jailer. Firecracker's production containment includes dropping privileges and restricting the process through namespaces and seccomp. One thing I sort of wished was touched on a little more: the concept of country is surprisingly modern. Modern international relations theory tends to trace the concept back to the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, but honestly, even that is really too early.

The map shown of 14th century Europe is doing better than most in that recognizes that several borders (but still too few) are fuzzy rather than lines on a map. The other problem you run into is that, in most non-state societies (in the Weberian sense of "monopoly on the legitimate use of force"), political linkages tend to be fragile and based more on personal ties so that a Big Man's successor may well repudiate the alliances and homages the Big Man makes. Which makes it hard to draw maps, because is Burgundy a part of France? The Duke of Burgundy is as often as not fighting the French king.

This is what makes adjudicating the "oldest continuous republic" hard, because at what point do we say that the homages San Marino is paying stops counting as being part of that country?

While the frontier (i.e. The toughest problems) will always push the limits of available computing power, what typical people do with AI won't always be on the frontier, nor will what appears on the frontier necessarily be lucrative. The frontier used to be playing Chess, Atari, and Go. These were challenging and really advanced AI, but they didn't make a lot of money. Now a phone can do these things.

You're an example of this process. You used to require a frontier model running on a data centre. Algorithms improved and, perhaps, your hardware as well, but your requirements didn't go up. Now you can do what you need to do with local hardware. You're one AI user who might not need to send money to Anthropic going forward unless you find a new frontier application that interests you.

This is why I'm a little bearish when it comes to the valuation of the AI giants. Yes, there are some extremely lucrative things on the frontier right now but, in the future, people may shift a lot of what they're doing now to local hardware while new things on the frontier may not produce the kind of profits that will pay back trillions in debt. Top #1 — the_panopticon:

For "Get used to the lack of a C standard library" mentioned in https://kevinboone.me/efitest4.html there's always https://github.com/tianocore/edk2-libc.

And on "Be aware of the Windows-ness of EFI" commentary the resemblance to Windows coding style https://computernewb.com/~lily/files/Documents/NTDesignWorkb... is no accident. We leveraged this coding methodology as we evolved the original Intel Boot Initiative then EFI and then UEFI code and specification https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/public/us/en/documents...

↳ reply 1 — PerryStyle:

There's also https://libc.llvm.org/uefi/index.html, but not sure if it's still receiving updates.

↳ reply 2 — FuriouslyAdrift:

Be aware EDK II has a recent severe CVE to watch out for.

https://app.opencve.io/cve/CVE-2026-97631

↳ reply 3 — kragen:

I think "leveraged this coding methodology" is an unjustifiably positive way to describe the results of the process. I think "spread this disease" would be more accurate. UTF-16 strings, really? VFAT? PE32+ is maybe justifiable (I'd prefer ELF, but that's because it's more familiar, not because it's actually better), but VFAT? And even in 01998 it should have been apparent that UTF-16 was not a sane format for strings, much less in 02005 when the EFI → UEFI transition happened.

To me, UEFI is like "leveraging the waste disposal methodology" of dumping your toxic waste in a lake. Yes, it's more convenient for you, but it does lasting damage and causes years of suffering for millions of people; and eventually somebody else has to clean up your mess, at far greater cost than if you'd just done something sensible to begin with.

I could probably say the same thing about X-Windows.

Top #2 — kevin_thibedeau:

> The linker won’t complain if your code calls functions that don’t exist – it will just mark them as external, expecting them to be provided by some other code. But they won’t be, and the program will just crash when it calls one of these missing functions.

You can verify no external symbols remain after linkage with: nm -D --undefined-only. This can be incorporated into a build script to verify the binary is valid.

Top #3 — JdeBP:

Rod Smith and the OSDev Wiki went here, sometimes word for word, years before:

* https://rodsbooks.com/efi-programming/

* https://wiki.osdev.org/GNU-EFI

Of course, they both assume GCC on Linux. Change either one of those, and it is a wholly different kettle of fish. Both NetBSD and FreeBSD, for examples, come with an EFI development environment in base, squirreled away in /usr/src/boot in the case of FreeBSD. They have to, because they need to be able to build their own EFI boot loaders. NetBSD targets more than Intel processor architectures for EFI, moreover. (NetBSD can boot via EFI on ARM CPUs, for instance.)

This is a natural progression (only on these types of projects). We accepted contributions because it actually helped and they were difficult and time consuming. Top #1 — Bender:

LLM bots are the easiest to spot. Rate limit them to 16kb/s and 1 request every 5 seconds. Give them a friendly multilingual WCAG status 429 page that says to slow down or status 444 and drop them into nftables ipsets if they continue to be aggressive. Ask your favorite LLM how to set this up. If your LLM gets session paused, ask Gemini or Grok. Tell it if you are behind a CDN. Enable logging of ssl curves, ciphers, etc... Show your LLM some examples from your access logs.

↳ reply 1 — eatonphil:

I get tens of thousands of IPs making 1 or 2 requests against pages on The Consensus (job search, code viewing, etc.). They're not super expensive pages. But I don't want to deal with the bot traffic (mostly because it messes up view counts I use to sell sponsorships). But then if I require an account (even a free one), valid readership is also going to drop with the new friction.

I could build something more complex to discover the patterns, or use Turnstile maybe. I'm not really sure at the moment.

↳↳ reply — EvanAnderson:

I mind a public access website for a government entity and this is exactly the pattern I see. US residential IPs make a couple of requests then never come back.

The bots may have layer 7 signatures that make them "easy" to block, but I'm dealing with COTS software with no ability to make changes to the stack. Even if I could by the time they're blocked the work is done and they're never coming back anyway.

I don't think I'm seeing the LLM bots in the scraping on this particular site. This site's data is highly sought-after by data brokers, legal services advertising, debt collectors, etc. I tend to think I'm seeing homespun scrapers. This site has been up for 20+ years and the scrapers seem to be well-adapted to using the HTML as an ad-hoc API for the data. The difference in the last few years has been the availability of vast numbers of residential proxies to mask the traffic.

↳ reply 2 — dmtroyer:

I think you overestimate many organizations ability to implement this type of rate-limiting.

Top #2 — blakesterz:

What I still don't understand is who is doing it? I assume it's not the big companies like OpenAI or Google or Anthropic, right? Is there an underground ecosystem where people buy and sell this stuff? I understand why it's valuable to the AI companies I'm curious about how all this work, the economics of it all.

↳ reply 1 — qingcharles:

Can't speak for everyone. I'm very gently scraping a lot of libraries for public domain periodical scans. The scans often exist nowhere else, or not in the same quality. Sometimes I find a certain library has perhaps the only known remaining intact copy of a periodical or a specific page.

The problem with the libraries is that all these scans are behind walls, so while the texts are public domain nobody can easily access them. I'm trying to liberate them and re-upload them outside the walls.

Until recently a lot of libraries would allow you to remotely sign up for a library card, but in the last 12 months almost all of them have reverted to having to bring ID in person to the library to validate your account, which puts the brakes on things.

↳↳ reply — sriacha:

I've been looking at historic newspapers recently, its bothersome and unfortunate that many (most?) are all behind newspapers.com (ancestry) paywall.

↳↳↳ reply — qingcharles:

Yeah, I'll be on ancestry.com and it says "We found this article about your great-grandfather!" and then you click it and it's newspapers.com and I have to close the tab.

What's the solution, though? All these newspapers won't scan themselves. I'm setting up a non-profit right now to deal with the magazines. The rights issues are both better and worse with magazines. "Better" in that most magazines have gone out of business and the rights are cheap. Worse in that most of them are orphans and the rights are very hard to track down.

↳ reply 2 — TazeTSchnitzel:

We're currently in the middle of an AI goldrush. There are probably hundreds of companies trying to do model pretraining. Anthropic and OpenAI and so on probably care about optics and implementing their crawlers properly. But there will be many firms few of us have heard of. I would guess some of them are Chinese, for example.

Top #3 — londons_explore:

Behind nearly every AI bot is some human who will see real benefit from scraping my site.

I just make sure all my pages are super lightweight to cache and serve from cloudflare and let the bots do what they like.

If I put something on the internet for all to see, I want bots to be able to see it too.

I've been on the other side of bot blocks - when I ask my LLM to buy me X and it comes back and says the only place it could buy from is some Bulgarian seller because everywhere else has anti-bot scripts, I make sure to give that Bulgarian site my business.

items.summary: 629 points, 1388 comments. See description for top comments.
